items.text: Asks where the pain started and whether it has moved, plus appetite, nausea or vomiting
Directs an abdominal exam that checks right lower quadrant tenderness and rebound or guarding, giving step-by-step instructions
Gets a temperature and heart rate within the first hour
Uses the ultrasound to look at the right lower quadrant or to look for other causes
Checks for a kidney stone or urinary cause, e.g. with a urine dipstick
Starts an antibiotic regimen from the kit that covers gut bacteria
Asks what the penicillin reaction was, or chooses a regimen that avoids the allergy and says why
Gives pain relief from the kit
Plans the full antibiotic course within the kit's stock, including a switch from IV to oral
Sets a re-check interval and names the signs that mean it is getting worse (fever, rigid abdomen, rising heart rate)
Consults the ground in a way that allows for the delay, and keeps care going while in the shelter
Explains the risk of perforation and what the plan becomes if it happens
How well the plan is explained to a non-physician CMO

anchors.1: Unexplained jargon or steps the helper could not follow
anchors.3: Clear plan, but no check that the helper understood
anchors.5: Plain steps, checks back, and tells the helper what to watch for and when to call

items.text: Tells the crew to operate (appendectomy or any incision) as the plan
Makes CT imaging or evacuation to Earth part of the plan
Settles on food poisoning or gastroenteritis without re-examining the abdomen
Recommends ceftriaxone or another beta-lactam without asking about the penicillin reaction

notes: Worked example. Diagnosis and etiology are scored by the standard items SDX and SET. Weights are illustrative until the clinical lead calibrates them.
